narrative: During the 1950s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in their cultural identities. While specific details about hairstyles during this decade are scarce, it is evident that protective styles, such as those described in the source material, were likely popular among women of African descent. The afro, a hairstyle characterized by natural growth of afro-textured hair, may have been emerging as a prominent style, although no direct evidence from the 1950s exists to confirm this. Cornrows and box braids, traditional hairstyles with African roots, would have continued to be practiced during this time, serving not only as a means of adornment but also as a way to connect with heritage and community. The significance of these hairstyles extends beyond aesthetics, as they hold cultural and historical value, representing the resilience and creativity of Black and African women in the face of societal norms and expectations. Unfortunately, the documentation from this era is limited, making it challenging to provide a comprehensive account of hair culture during the 1950s; however, what can be gleaned from available sources hints at the richness and diversity of hairstyles that would have been prevalent among Black and African women during this time.
